name: IBPS Clerk
fullName: Institute of Banking Personnel Selection – Common Recruitment Process for Customer Service Associates (CRP CSA / Clerk)
eligibility: Graduate in any discipline; 20–28 years (relaxation for reserved categories); proficiency in the official language of the state applied for

notification.summary: CRP CSA-XVI (Clerk 2026) notification came out in late July 2026 with online registration from 1 to 21 Aug 2026. The preliminary exam is scheduled for 10–11 Oct 2026 (in progress on the check date) and the mains is reported for 27 Dec 2026 (tentative). Dates are from news/education portals because ibps.in could not be reached from the research environment.

pattern.notes: 20 minutes per section with a separate timer. Sectional and overall cut-offs (state-wise) apply; prelims is qualifying only. No interview — final selection is on mains marks. Scores are normalised across shifts.

trendAnalysis.summary: The clerk prelims is easy-to-moderate; good attempts are usually 70–80. Numerical Ability is speed-driven: simplification/approximation (10–15 Qs), number series (5) and one or two DI sets, with the rest as short arithmetic word problems. Reasoning has 3–4 small puzzles/seating arrangements (box, floor, day-based, linear) carrying 12–15 questions, plus syllogism, inequality, coding, blood relations and quick misc questions. English is based on one RC (≈8–10 Qs), cloze, error spotting, fillers and rearrangement; word-swap and connector formats appeared more often recently.

pyqBlueprint.method: Compiled from shift-wise memory-based analyses of IBPS Clerk (CRP CSA) prelims 2023, 2024 and 2025 (4–5 Oct 2025 shifts) published by coaching sites (Time4Education, Physics Wallah, Adda247, Mahendras), cross-checked with the official IBPS prelims pattern. Patterns are paraphrased in our own words; no real question is reproduced.

archetypes.pattern: RC set (about 300–400 words, simple social/economic theme): identify the central idea or the most suitable title; distractors are partial details
RC fact-check: 'Which of the following is true / NOT true according to the passage' — one option distorts a qualifier (some→most, may→will) or reverses cause and effect
RC inference with statements I, II, III and combination options (Only I / Only I and III …); the trap statement overstates what the passage says
RC vocabulary-in-context: synonym or antonym of a word used in the passage, with distractors that are dictionary meanings not fitting the context
Passage cloze with numbered blanks; five same-part-of-speech options where distractors are look-alike or collocation-breaking words
Sentence split into parts (A)–(D) plus 'No error' (E); errors in subject–verb agreement, prepositions, pronouns, tense, comparatives, or inversion after negative adverbs
Double filler: two blanks in one sentence, five word-pairs where one word of each wrong pair fits but the other does not
Single filler: one blank, five words close in meaning; only one matches the tone/collocation of the sentence
Para jumble of five or six sentences on one theme; choose the correct order (options are sequences); connectors like 'however', 'as a result' and pronouns fix the order
Para jumble asking which sentence comes FIRST / THIRD / LAST after rearrangement (options are sentence letters)
Word swap: four highlighted words in a sentence; identify the pair whose interchange makes the sentence correct, or 'No interchange required'
Phrase replacement: a highlighted phrase with a grammar/idiom error; choose the correct replacement, or 'No replacement required'
Vocabulary & spelling: choose the correctly or incorrectly spelt word among five commonly confused spellings, or a simple synonym/antonym
Connector: choose the word/phrase that joins two sentences without changing the meaning (cause, contrast, condition)
Table DI (5 rows × 2–3 columns): percentage increase/decrease of one entity between two years, or one entity as a percentage of another
Table DI with a percentage column (e.g. share of a sub-category): compute derived values (sum, average, difference or ratio of derived quantities)
Caselet DI: a paragraph giving a total and splits in ratios/percentages; questions combine two splits or ask what changes after a transfer
Bar-graph / line-graph DI (values for 5–6 months or items given): average, ratio, and percentage more/less between two bars
Missing number series built on differences of squares/cubes, alternate ×n +k, or ×n with increasing n
Wrong number series: one term breaks the ×/+ pattern; find it
Exact simplification with BODMAS, percentages, fractions, squares and square roots; find '?'
Approximation: decimals close to whole numbers in %, ×, ÷, √ and powers; find the nearest value
Find the unknown placed inside the expression (? % of N, √?, ?² or a fraction of ?)
Profit & loss with marked price, discount and cost price (single or successive discounts, 'had he sold for ₹x more')
Percentage word problem: income–expenditure–savings, successive percentage change, or one value as a percentage of another
Ages: present-age ratio with a condition some years before/after; find an age or sum of ages
Ratio & proportion: dividing an amount in a ratio, or changing a ratio by adding/removing a quantity
Time & work / pipes: efficiencies combined, one leaves after some days, or an emptying pipe
Trains crossing poles/platforms/each other, relative speed, or average speed of a round trip
Boats and streams: downstream/upstream speeds and times
Simple vs compound interest: CI–SI difference, amount at CI, or a sum split between two rates
Mixture & alligation: mixing two varieties to a target price/ratio, or adding/replacing liquid
Mensuration: rectangle/circle/cylinder area, perimeter or volume relationships
Average: one member removed/added or replaced, find the new average or the member's value
Linear row of 6–8 persons facing north (occasionally with a vacant seat); direct clues on ends and 'only n persons between'
Circular table (6–8 persons) facing the centre (or some outside); left/right relations and 'second to the left of' questions
Floor-based puzzle (5–8 floors, sometimes two flats per floor) with a second attribute such as colour/city/fruit
Scheduling puzzle: persons/events on days of the week or months (sometimes with dates 1xth/2xth); 'how many between' questions
Box stacking: boxes placed one above another, with colour/item attribute and 'how many boxes between' clues
Comparison puzzle: heights/weights/marks of 5–6 persons with 'more than only' clues; ask rank or a derived value
Syllogism with 2–3 statements and two conclusions, including 'possibility' conclusions; standard five options
Syllogism with 'Only a few' or 'No' statements where a definite 'All' conclusion is the trap
Direct inequality: two or three combined statements, two conclusions to check
Blood relation chain or 'pointing to a photograph' statement; gender ambiguity is the usual trap
Direction & distance: a person walks a path with left/right turns; find the shortest distance and direction from start
Point-based direction: several points given relative to each other; find direction/distance between two of them
Letter coding: word coded by letter shifts / reversal / opposite letters; code a new word
Sentence (Chinese) coding: three or four phrases coded in two-letter codes; find the code of a word by elimination
Order & ranking: positions from both ends of a row/class, total count, or persons between two people
Alphanumeric-symbol arrangement: count elements satisfying a 'preceded by / followed by' condition, or find the nth element from an end
English alphabet positions: nth letter from left/right after rearrangement or reversal; letter-pair series
Letter pairs in a word with as many letters between them as in the English alphabet
Number formation: digits of 3-digit numbers rearranged/operated on; find the resulting number or difference
Odd one out among numbers, words or letter groups
Direction after a sequence of clockwise/anticlockwise turns in degrees

resources.notes: IBPS does not release full question papers or answer keys for the clerk exam. Official material is limited to the Information Handout with sample questions and the pre-exam online practice test on ibps.in; candidates see their own scorecard. Previous papers in circulation are memory-based compilations by coaching portals.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

Cities are getting hotter faster than the countryside around them. Concrete, asphalt and glass absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night, so urban neighbourhoods often stay several degrees warmer than nearby villages after sunset. This 'heat island' effect is not merely uncomfortable; it raises electricity demand for cooling, worsens air quality and can be deadly for outdoor workers and the elderly. Fortunately, some remedies are cheap. Painting roofs white reflects a large share of sunlight, and planting trees along streets provides both shade and cooling through evaporation. Several Indian cities have begun drafting heat action plans that combine such measures with early warnings and changes in working hours during heatwaves. Experts, however, caution that these plans succeed only when they are funded and enforced, not when they remain documents on a shelf.

According to the passage, why do urban neighbourhoods stay warmer than villages after sunset?
options: Cities receive more sunlight than villages
Concrete, asphalt and glass release the heat they absorbed during the day slowly
Trees in cities trap heat at night
questions.explanation: The passage says these materials 'absorb sunlight during the day and release it slowly at night'.

relevance.note: Heat-island detail question; Clerk RC does ask cause lookups though passage is short (~150 words)

relevance.note: Vocab-in-context 'caution'='warn'; 'doubt' as near trap; clerk standard

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
He has been working (A)/ in this bank since (B)/ the last five years (C)/ and plans to retire soon. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: A period of time ('the last five years') takes 'for', not 'since'. The error is in part B ('since' should be 'for').

relevance.note: 'since' (in part B) should be 'for' with a period; frequent clerk error-spotting item

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error.
Each of the candidates (A)/ were asked to bring (B)/ two photographs and (C)/ a valid identity proof. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Each of the…' is singular and takes 'was', so 'were asked' in part B is wrong.

relevance.note: 'Each of ... were' agreement; standard clerk error item (labelled hard but easy)

questions.question:
Choose the pair that best fills both blanks.
The ______ rains damaged the standing crops, leaving farmers in ______.
questions.explanation: Rain that damages crops is 'unseasonal', and it leaves farmers 'in distress'. Other pairs are illogical.

relevance.note: Double filler unseasonal/distress; acceptable clerk pair though distractors weak

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a meaningful paragraph and choose the FOURTH sentence.
A. She saved a small amount from her earnings every week.
B. Meena started a tailoring unit with a single sewing machine.
C. Today, her unit employs twelve women from her village.
D. Within two years, she had enough to buy three more machines.
E. She also took a small loan from a self-help group.
questions.explanation: Order: B (start) – A (savings) – E ('also' a loan) – D (bought machines) – C (today). Fourth sentence is D.

relevance.note: Story jumble asking FOURTH sentence (BAEDC); clerk-faithful

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a meaningful paragraph.
A. Therefore, it is wise to compare offers before signing up.
B. Credit cards can be useful if used responsibly.
C. However, they often carry very high interest on unpaid balances.
D. Fees and reward programmes also differ widely between banks.
E. They let users make purchases now and pay later.
questions.explanation: B introduces credit cards, E gives the benefit, C ('However') the drawback, D ('also') adds another difference, A ('Therefore') concludes: BECDA.

questions.question:
Choose the option that should replace the phrase in capitals to make the sentence correct.
She is SENIOR THAN ME in the office.
questions.explanation: Adjectives of Latin origin such as senior, junior and superior take 'to', not 'than': 'senior to me'.

relevance.note: 'senior to' idiom replacement; classic clerk item
Fraction-of-fraction with ? inside; matches Q13 clerk type

questions.question:
What approximate value should come in place of '?'
24.97 × 16.02 − 179.98 ÷ 5.99 ≈ ?

What approximate value should come in place of '?'
63.89% of 449.95 + √1023.8 × 7.01 ≈ ?

relevance.note: Approximation with % and root*number; clerk standard

questions.question: Find the next term: 5, 11, 23, 47, 95, ?
questions.explanation: Each term = previous × 2 + 1. 95 × 2 + 1 = 191.

questions.question: Find the next term: 120, 119, 115, 106, 90, ?
questions.explanation: Differences are −1, −4, −9, −16 (squares); next −25: 90 − 25 = 65.

questions.question: Find the next term: 7, 7, 14, 42, 168, ?

The number of savings accounts opened (in hundreds) by a bank branch in five months was: January 24, February 30, March 36, April 27, May 33.

The accounts opened in April are what percent less than those opened in March?

relevance.note: Percent-less between bars; good trap with 25% vs 33.3%

questions.question:
The number of savings accounts opened (in hundreds) by a bank branch in five months was: January 24, February 30, March 36, April 27, May 33.

What is the ratio of accounts opened in February and April together to those opened in March and May together?

relevance.note: Ratio of paired sums with 57:67 near-distractor

questions.question: A man sells two watches for ₹1,200 each. On one he gains 20% and on the other he loses 20%. What is his overall result?

relevance.note: Equal SP +-x% loss; classic clerk P&L

questions.question: The sum of the ages of a father and his son is 50 years. Five years ago the father was seven times as old as the son. What is the father's present age?

relevance.note: Father-son sum and past multiple; clerk ages

questions.question: 12 men can finish a job in 15 days working 8 hours a day. In how many days will 20 men finish it working 6 hours a day?
questions.explanation: Total = 12 × 15 × 8 = 1440 man-hours. 20 men × 6 h = 120 per day → 1440/120 = 12 days.

questions.question: A 240 m long train passes a pole in 12 seconds. How long will it take to cross a 360 m long platform?

relevance.note: Train pole to platform; clerk staple

questions.question: The simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 8% per annum is ₹1,440. What is the compound interest (compounded annually) on the same sum for 2 years at 10% per annum?

relevance.note: SI to principal then CI; clerk standard

questions.question: The average of five numbers is 42. If one number, 30, is removed, what is the average of the remaining numbers?

Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T and U are placed one above another (position 1 is the bottom, 6 the top). R is placed fourth from the bottom. Only two boxes are placed between R and S. T is placed immediately above Q. U is not placed adjacent to S. P is placed somewhere below Q.

Which box is placed immediately below R?
questions.explanation: Bottom to top: S, P, U, R, Q, T. R is 4th, so S is 1st; Q–T must be 5th–6th (Q at 2nd would leave no place below it for P); U cannot be 2nd (adjacent to S), so U is 3rd and P 2nd. U is below R.

questions.question:
Six boxes P, Q, R, S, T and U are placed one above another (position 1 is the bottom, 6 the top). R is placed fourth from the bottom. Only two boxes are placed between R and S. T is placed immediately above Q. U is not placed adjacent to S. P is placed somewhere below Q.

How many boxes are placed between P and T?
questions.explanation: Bottom to top: S, P, U, R, Q, T. Between P (2nd) and T (6th) are U, R and Q — three boxes.

questions.question:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F attend a workshop on six consecutive days from Monday to Saturday, one person per day. B attends on Thursday. Only two persons attend between B and D. A attends on the day immediately after D. F attends on some day before E. C attends on some day after E.

Who attends the workshop on Wednesday?
questions.explanation: B is on Thursday, so D (three days away) is on Monday and A on Tuesday. F, E, C take Wednesday, Friday, Saturday in that order (F before E before C). F is on Wednesday.

questions.question:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F attend a workshop on six consecutive days from Monday to Saturday, one person per day. B attends on Thursday. Only two persons attend between B and D. A attends on the day immediately after D. F attends on some day before E. C attends on some day after E.

How many persons attend between A and E?
questions.explanation: Order: D (Mon), A (Tue), F (Wed), B (Thu), E (Fri), C (Sat). Between A and E are F and B — two persons.

questions.question:
Six friends A, B, C, D, E and F attend a workshop on six consecutive days from Monday to Saturday, one person per day. B attends on Thursday. Only two persons attend between B and D. A attends on the day immediately after D. F attends on some day before E. C attends on some day after E.

Who attends immediately before C?
questions.explanation: Order: D, A, F, B, E, C. E attends on Friday, just before C on Saturday.

questions.question:
Statements: Some pens are pencils. No pencil is an eraser.
Conclusions: I. Some pens are not erasers. II. Some erasers are pens.
questions.explanation: The pens that are pencils cannot be erasers, so I follows. There is no definite link between erasers and pens, so II does not follow.

relevance.note: Some/No with 'Some pens are not erasers' follows; clerk standard

questions.question:
Statement: M ≥ N > O = P ≤ Q
Conclusions: I. M > P  II. Q ≥ O
questions.explanation: M ≥ N > O = P gives M > P. Q ≥ P = O gives Q ≥ O. Both follow.

questions.question:
Statement: R < S ≤ T = U > V ≥ W
Conclusions: I. S < U  II. T > W
questions.explanation: S ≤ T = U gives S ≤ U, so 'S < U' is not definite (I fails). T = U > V ≥ W gives T > W (II follows).

relevance.note: S<=U vs strict S<U trap; good

questions.question: In a certain code, 'GARDEN' is written as 'FBQEDO'. How is 'MARKET' written in that code?
questions.explanation: Letters alternately move −1, +1: G−1=F, A+1=B, R−1=Q, D+1=E, E−1=D, N+1=O. MARKET → L, B, Q, L, D, U = LBQLDU.

questions.question: Pointing to a woman, Aman said, 'She is the only daughter of my paternal grandfather's only son.' How is the woman related to Aman?
questions.explanation: The only son of Aman's paternal grandfather is Aman's father; his only daughter is Aman's sister.

questions.question:
Arrangement: B 7 # D 3 K @ 9 M 2 $ P 5 R & 8 T
Which element is 4th to the right of the 10th element from the left?
questions.explanation: The 10th element from the left is 2; the 4th to its right is the 14th element, R.

relevance.note: nth from end in symbol arrangement; clerk standard

questions.question: If the English alphabet is written in reverse order (Z to A), which letter will be 8th to the right of the 15th letter from the left?
questions.explanation: In reverse order, position k holds the letter numbered 27 − k. 15 + 8 = 23rd position → letter number 4 = D.

relevance.note: Reverse alphabet position; clerk R23 standard

questions.question: In the number 5726436, 1 is added to each odd digit and 1 is subtracted from each even digit. How many digits appear more than once in the new number?
questions.explanation: 5→6, 7→8, 2→1, 6→5, 4→3, 3→4, 6→5 gives 6815345. Only 5 appears twice, so one digit repeats.

relevance.note: Digit operation and repeats; clerk misc type

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.

In many Indian cities, residents depend on water tankers during the summer months, paying high prices for water that is often of doubtful quality. Yet the same cities receive heavy rain for a few months every year, most of which simply runs off roads into drains. Rooftop rainwater harvesting offers a simple way to capture some of this water. Rain falling on a roof is collected through pipes, filtered through layers of sand and gravel, and either stored in a tank or sent down a recharge pit to refill the groundwater below.

The cost of such a system is modest compared with what a family spends on tankers in a single dry season. In several housing societies that adopted it, borewells that had dried up began to yield water again within two or three years. However, the benefits depend on regular care. Filters clogged with leaves and silt can stop working, and pits that are not cleaned before the monsoon may overflow.

Experts therefore say that rules making rainwater harvesting compulsory for new buildings are only a first step. Residents also need to understand how the systems work and who is responsible for maintaining them.

Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
options: Rooftop rainwater harvesting is a low-cost way to ease urban water shortages, but it works only when the systems are maintained
Water tankers are the best solution to water shortages in Indian cities
Rainwater harvesting is too expensive for most families
Compulsory rules have already solved the water problem in cities
Borewells should be banned in housing societies
questions.explanation: The passage explains how harvesting captures wasted rain cheaply and then stresses that regular maintenance and awareness are needed for it to work.

relevance.note: Rainwater harvesting main idea with over-generalisation distractors

Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
I. Most of the rain that falls on cities is currently wasted as run-off.
II. Making harvesting compulsory for new buildings is, by itself, enough to solve the problem.
III. Buying water from tankers can be costly for families.

questions.question:
Read the passage and choose the word that best fits the numbered blank.

Learning to manage money is a skill that is rarely taught in schools. Many young people open their first bank account only after they start (1) ______, and they often learn about interest, loans and credit cards through costly mistakes. Some banks have now begun to (2) ______ free workshops in colleges, where students learn to make a monthly budget and to spot (3) ______ messages that try to steal their banking details.

Which word best fits blank (2)?
questions.explanation: Banks 'conduct' (organise) workshops in colleges. 'Attend' would make the banks the learners; 'cancel/avoid/deny' contradict 'where students learn'.

questions.question:
Read the passage and choose the word that best fits the numbered blank.

Learning to manage money is a skill that is rarely taught in schools. Many young people open their first bank account only after they start (1) ______, and they often learn about interest, loans and credit cards through costly mistakes. Some banks have now begun to (2) ______ free workshops in colleges, where students learn to make a monthly budget and to spot (3) ______ messages that try to steal their banking details.

Which word best fits blank (3)?
questions.explanation: Messages that 'try to steal banking details' are fraudulent; the other adjectives describe safe messages.

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose 'E'.
The number of customers (A)/ who uses mobile banking (B)/ has increased sharply (C)/ over the last year. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: 'Who' refers to 'customers' (plural), so the verb should be 'use'. The error is in part B. ('The number … has increased' is correct.)

relevance.note: 'who uses' relative clause agreement; faithful clerk trap

questions.question:
Find the part of the sentence that has an error. If there is no error, choose 'E'.
If I was you, (A)/ I would open (B)/ a recurring deposit (C)/ without any delay. (D)/ No error (E)
questions.explanation: Imaginary conditions take the subjunctive 'were': 'If I were you'. The error is in part A.

questions.question:
Choose the word that best fills the blank.
The doctor advised him to ______ from eating fried food for a few weeks.
questions.explanation: Only 'refrain' is used with 'from' + -ing in this sense ('refrain from eating'). 'Avoid eating', 'stop eating' and 'quit eating' do not take 'from'; 'prevent' needs an object.

questions.question:
Rearrange the sentences to form a meaningful paragraph and choose the LAST sentence.
A. It is therefore wise to keep your phone's software updated.
B. Mobile phones today store much of our personal and banking information.
C. Software updates often fix security weaknesses that criminals could exploit.
D. Losing such information to hackers can cause serious financial harm.
E. Many people, however, ignore update alerts for months.
questions.explanation: Order: B – D – C – E – A. Sentence A, beginning with 'therefore', draws the conclusion and comes last.

questions.question:
Which pair of words should be interchanged to make the sentence meaningful?
The (A) clerk posted the (B) deadline to the (C) customer before the (D) letter.
questions.explanation: Swapping B and D: 'The clerk posted the letter to the customer before the deadline.'

questions.question:
What approximate value should come in place of '?'
24.98 × 18.03 + 399.9 ÷ 7.98 ≈ ?

questions.question:
The number of two-wheeler loans disbursed by a bank branch in six months was: January – 240, February – 180, March – 300, April – 270, May – 210, June – 360.

By what percentage did the number of loans increase from February to March?
questions.explanation: Increase = 300 − 180 = 120. 120/180 × 100 = 66⅔%. (40% is 120 as a percentage of 300 — the usual trap.)

questions.question:
The number of two-wheeler loans disbursed by a bank branch in six months was: January – 240, February – 180, March – 300, April – 270, May – 210, June – 360.

What is the ratio of the loans disbursed in January and April together to those disbursed in May and June together?
questions.explanation: January + April = 510; May + June = 570. 510 : 570 = 17 : 19.

questions.question: The present ages of a mother and her daughter are in the ratio 8 : 3. After 6 years, the mother will be twice as old as the daughter. What is the daughter's present age?
questions.explanation: (8k + 6) = 2(3k + 6) → 2k = 6 → k = 3. Daughter = 3 × 3 = 9 years (mother 24).

questions.question: 15 men can complete a work in 24 days. They work for 8 days, after which 5 more men join them. In how many more days will the remaining work be completed?
questions.explanation: Total work = 15 × 24 = 360 man-days; done in 8 days = 120. Remaining 240 man-days with 20 men → 12 days.

questions.question: A train 180 m long running at 54 km/h crosses a platform in 20 seconds. What is the length of the platform?
questions.explanation: Speed = 54 × 5/18 = 15 m/s. Distance in 20 s = 300 m = train + platform → platform = 120 m.

Eight persons P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W sit in a straight row, all facing north.
S sits third from the left end. Only two persons sit between S and V. W sits immediately to the right of V. P sits at one of the extreme ends and only one person sits between P and V. Q sits immediately to the left of S. T sits immediately to the left of V. U is not an immediate neighbour of S.

Who sits second to the right of R?
questions.explanation: Left to right: U, Q, S, R, T, V, W, P. Second to the right of R is V.

questions.question:
Eight persons P, Q, R, S, T, U, V and W sit in a straight row, all facing north.
S sits third from the left end. Only two persons sit between S and V. W sits immediately to the right of V. P sits at one of the extreme ends and only one person sits between P and V. Q sits immediately to the left of S. T sits immediately to the left of V. U is not an immediate neighbour of S.

How many persons sit between U and T?
questions.explanation: U is 1st and T is 5th from the left; Q, S and R sit between them — three persons.

questions.question:
Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G attend a training programme on seven different days of the same week, from Monday to Sunday.
Only three persons attend after D. G attends immediately before D. Only one person attends between G and E, and E attends before G. B attends on some day before D. Only one person attends between A and C. C does not attend on Friday.

Who attends the training on Saturday?
questions.explanation: Monday – E, Tuesday – B, Wednesday – G, Thursday – D, Friday – A, Saturday – F, Sunday – C.

questions.question:
Seven persons A, B, C, D, E, F and G attend a training programme on seven different days of the same week, from Monday to Sunday.
Only three persons attend after D. G attends immediately before D. Only one person attends between G and E, and E attends before G. B attends on some day before D. Only one person attends between A and C. C does not attend on Friday.

How many persons attend between B and A?
questions.explanation: B attends on Tuesday and A on Friday; G and D attend in between — two persons.

questions.question:
Six persons J, K, L, M, N and O are of different heights. K is taller than only two persons. J is taller than M but shorter than N. M is taller than K. O is shorter than L.

Who is the second shortest person?
questions.explanation: Tallest to shortest: N, J, M, K, L, O. The second shortest is L.

questions.question:
Six persons J, K, L, M, N and O are of different heights. K is taller than only two persons. J is taller than M but shorter than N. M is taller than K. O is shorter than L.

If the tallest person is 180 cm tall and K is 165 cm tall, which of the following can be J's height?
questions.explanation: Order: N (180) > J > M > K (165). J must be between 165 cm and 180 cm (and above M), so only 178 cm is possible.

questions.question:
Statements: All pens are markers. Some markers are erasers.
Conclusions: I. Some pens are erasers. II. Some erasers are markers.
questions.explanation: Pens and erasers have no definite link, so I does not follow. 'Some markers are erasers' converts to 'Some erasers are markers', so II follows.

questions.question:
Statements: Only a few cards are coins. All coins are notes.
Conclusions: I. Some cards are notes. II. All cards are notes.
questions.explanation: The cards that are coins are notes, so I follows. The cards that are not coins may or may not be notes, so the definite statement II does not follow.

questions.question:
Statement: P ≥ Q > R = S ≤ T
Conclusions: I. P > S  II. T > R
questions.explanation: P ≥ Q > R = S gives P > S, so I follows. T ≥ S = R gives only T ≥ R, so II (T > R) does not follow.

questions.question: In a certain code, 'BRANCH' is written as 'CQBMDG'. How is 'CREDIT' written in that code?
questions.explanation: Letters are shifted alternately +1 and −1: B+1 = C, R−1 = Q, A+1 = B, N−1 = M, C+1 = D, H−1 = G. So CREDIT → D Q F C J S.

questions.question: In a code language, 'save money daily' is written as 'la ki po', 'money grows daily' is written as 'po ri ki' and 'grows with time' is written as 'ri ne su'. What is the code for 'save'?
questions.explanation: 'money' and 'daily' are common to the first two sentences, so they take 'ki' and 'po'. The remaining code in the first sentence, 'la', means 'save'.

questions.question: Amit walks 20 m towards the east, turns right and walks 15 m, turns right again and walks 30 m, and then turns right and walks 15 m. How far and in which direction is he from his starting point?
questions.explanation: East 20, south 15, west 30, north 15. Net: 10 m to the west, with no north–south displacement.

questions.question:

Which element is 5th to the right of the 8th element from the left end?
questions.explanation: The 8th element from the left is 9. Counting 5 to its right: B, 2, #, N, 5 → 5.

questions.question: If the letters of the word 'PLANET' are arranged in alphabetical order from left to right, how many letters will remain in the same position?
questions.explanation: PLANET → AELNPT. N (4th) and T (6th) stay in place — two letters.
